sections.title: Front matter

summary.text: Title, authors and abstract of "Evaluating Large Language Models for Public Health Classification and Extraction Tasks" by Joshua Harris and colleagues at the UK Health Security Agency. Six external and seven newly annotated datasets are combined into 16 tasks on health burden, epidemiological risk factors and public health interventions, and eleven open-weight LLMs (7-123 billion parameters) are evaluated with zero-shot prompting. Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct is best on 8 of 16 tasks by micro-F1; every open-weight model scores below 60% on some tasks, such as Contact Classification, and above 80% on others, such as GI Illness Classification. On 11 tasks, three GPT-4 and GPT-4o models give results comparable to Llama-3.3-70B. Figure 1 shows the three evaluation areas and each model family's scores.

sections.title: Introduction

summary.text: Introduction. LLM performance varies widely by model and task, so applying LLMs in public health first needs domain-specific evaluations representative of the tasks, text and knowledge experts meet, and the aim is to learn what drives the variation: the model, the task, the text type or the implementation. This initial work covers automated evaluation (excluding LLM-as-a-judge) of natural language understanding tasks such as classification, using in-context learning only. The evaluations are meant to support continual assessment of new models, identify areas where LLMs could be applied, and give a baseline for future fine-tuning; long-form generation tasks judged by experts, and issues such as bias, are left for further work.

sections.extract: There have been rapid improvements in the ability of Large Language Models (LLMs)1 to perform a broad range of text processing tasks [3, 4, 5]. This has led to significant interest in applying them to support experts across a range of domains [6], including public health [7, 8, 9]. sections.title: Methods

summary.text: Methods overview. Evaluation methodology depends on the level of generality, the type of task and the outcome of interest (reviewed in Section 6), and the paper aims for a broad, automated assessment of classification and extraction tasks. Its components are seven new datasets annotated with public health specialists from internal, synthetic and external text; six existing datasets from prior work; 16 evaluation tasks across three public health sub-domains (Figure 1); and eleven open-weight models from 7 to 123 billion parameters, with three GPT-4 series models (turbo, 4o and 4o-mini) on a subset of 11 tasks for comparison with leading private models.

sections.extract: Evaluation of LLMs is a broad and rapidly growing field of research [15] ranging from very general assessments of capabilities or intelligence [3] to very task specific performance results [17] (Fig. 5). We focus on domain and task specific evaluations of LLMs within public health and provide a review of the relevant literature in Sec. 6. sections.title: Public Health Evaluation Tasks and Datasets

summary.text: The opening of the task and dataset section: because public health spans many fields beyond healthcare, the 16 classification and extraction tasks cover a broad range within three sub-domains, introduced next.

sections.extract: Public health is a broad field, intersecting with many different fields and issues in addition to conditions treated within healthcare settings [18, 19, 20, 21]. Therefore, to ensure our evaluations are representative, the 16 classification and extraction tasks we bring together target a commensurately broad range of tasks within three key sub-domains of public health:

sections.title: Burden

summary.text: Burden tasks, with Figure 2 (tasks by area) and Table 1 (all 16 tasks with dataset, type, test-set size, text type, average length, example labels and whether annotations are public). Text sources range from academic literature to social media, news and questionnaires. The burden tasks are NCBI Disease Extraction, scored on de-duplicated MeSH and OMIM codes to ease exact-match problems; Gastrointestinal Illness Classification on about 3,000 Yelp restaurant reviews pre-filtered by GI keywords, which makes it adversarial since every "no" review contains such a keyword; GI Illness Symptom Extraction from the reviews annotated as possible illness; ICD-10 Description Classification of whether a description refers to an infection or a primarily infectious disease, on a balanced sample annotated by two analysts; and News Headline Classification of GDELT headlines about avian influenza, five at a time with JSON output. An MMLU Virology task was removed after later work questioned that subset's error rate.

sections.extract: The range of data used in our evaluation is also broad, because potentially relevant health information is found in a diverse range of sources: academic literature, electronic health records, public health guidance, social media, news articles, and questionnaire responses [22]. sections.title: Risk Factors

summary.text: Risk-factor tasks. Contact Type Classification uses a new synthetic dataset generated with GPT-4 in the style of mpox contact-tracing questionnaires and manually annotated; it is hard because the model must apply a detailed protocol given in the prompt, and because the text often discusses sexual activity, which many training datasets avoid. Country Disambiguation maps anonymised place-of-birth answers from GP registration forms, which automated matching failed on, to a country or "unknown", standardised with the country-converter package. Food Extraction pulls foods from the GI-annotated Yelp reviews and maps them through a FoodEx 2 lookup to 27 labels relevant to foodborne illness. MMLU Medical Genetics and MMLU Nutrition test basic knowledge by multiple choice.

sections.extract: Epidemiological risk factors are environmental, behavioral, or biological factors that increase a person’s likelihood of developing disease or injury [36]. Risk factor surveillance is essential for quantifying these risks and developing evidence-based interventions to reduce them [37]. summary.text: The opening of the interventions section. Interventions are commonly split into pharmaceutical ones, such as vaccination, and non-pharmaceutical ones that reduce behavioural risk factors, such as nutrition advice or hand hygiene. Since guidance is a primary way interventions are communicated, the authors introduce four guidance-related evaluations of increasing difficulty, plus tasks on pharmaceutical interventions and biomedical reasoning. sections.title: Summary

summary.text: The intervention tasks, continued (the extraction places them under a "Summary" heading), and the task summary. Guidance Topic Classification assigns UKHSA gov.uk summary pages to one of eight health topics by authoring team. Guidance Recommendation Classification asks yes or no whether a chunk of UKHSA guidance contains a clear actionable recommendation, on 489 annotated chunks. Health Advice Classification labels PubMed sentences as no, weak or strong advice (HealthAdvice, 10,845 sentences), and Health Causal Claims Classification labels PubMed conclusion sentences as no relation, correlational, conditional causal or direct causal. BioDex Drugs Extraction takes the drugs in adverse drug event reports from 1,558 articles chunked to at most 6,000 characters, and PubMedQA answers an abstract's title question yes, no or maybe in the reasoning-required setting. The summary notes the balance of general and public-health-specific tasks and of external and internal datasets.

sections.title: Large Language Models

summary.text: Large language models. The table caption explains that open-weight models are hosted internally for comparability and data protection, in FP16 where feasible, with GPT-4 models on a subset of tasks. The eleven open-weight models span 7 to 123 billion parameters across the Llama-2 and 3, Mistral, Command-R, Gemma and Flan-T5 families, and the effect of INT-4 quantization is studied on the Llama-3 family. Models run on an internal API on UKHSA high-performance computing with HuggingFace models, transformers and vLLM, which lets restricted datasets stay on UKHSA systems and keeps quantisation, prompt templates, versions and generation settings under control. GPT-4 Turbo and GPT-4o are accessed through the OpenAI API, but not on all tasks, mainly because of data restrictions; the block ends mid-sentence.

summary.text: Prompting and sampling (the extraction places them under a "Results" heading). Zero-shot results are reported for every task, with few-shot prompting also studied on some harder tasks. The model authors' prompt templates are used where available, which varies prompt content somewhat, for example in system prompts, while keeping the informational content as consistent as possible. summary.text: Dataset splits: a 20-80 validation-test split for every task, with only the validation set used for prompt development so the prompts are not overfitted to the test set used to report performance.

sections.extract: We use a 20-80 validation-test split for all tasks, where only the validation set is used for prompt development; this avoids overfitting the prompt to the test set, which we use to quantify performance in this paper. 2.2.5

sections.title: Evaluation Metrics

summary.text: Evaluation metrics, the start of the results, and Table 3. Micro- and macro-F1 are reported, micro-F1 being the headline (for single-label classification it equals accuracy). Extraction uses exact string matching, with outputs outside the label set counted as incorrect; classification uses exact matching after light clean-up, with more advanced standardisation for Country Disambiguation, NCBI Disease Extraction and Food Extraction. Open-weight models are discussed first since they ran on every task. Table 3 gives zero-shot micro-F1 for the eleven open-weight models on the 16 tasks: Llama-3.3-70B has the best mean task rank (2.50), followed by Llama-3.1-70B (2.94) and Llama-3-70B (3.12), and Mistral-Large was run in INT-4 AWQ.

sections.extract: In this paper we primarily report the micro and macro F1 scores for each task. The F1 score is calculated as the harmonic mean of precision3 (positive predictive value) and recall4 (sensitivity). The micro-F1 score is calculated by weighting each label according to its frequency in the dataset, while the macro-F1 score is calculated weighting each label equally. sections.title: Model Results

summary.text: Model results. Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct is the highest or equal highest open-weight model on 8 of the 16 tasks. Flan-T5-xxl, Llama-3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B were each worst on at least one task, and the authors note that smaller models seem more fragile to prompt wording, so a low score may reflect misreading the prompt rather than inability. Scaling from Llama-3-8B to Llama-3-70B adds more than 10 percentage points on MMLU Genetics, MMLU Nutrition, Health Advice and Causal Relations, and moving from a Llama-2-70B to a Llama-3-70B base also helps; each Llama 3 70B version has a better mean task rank than the last. Mistral-Large's relatively weak results may stem from its INT-4 quantization.

sections.title: Task Results

summary.text: Task results. Performance varies greatly across tasks: every model scores at least 85% micro-F1 on ICD-10 Description Classification, and above 80% on GI Illness Classification, Country Disambiguation and Food Extraction, but no model exceeds 60% on BioDex Drugs Extraction or Contact Classification with zero-shot prompts.

sections.extract: We find significant variability in performance across tasks. For tasks like ICD-10 Description Classification all of the models classify text with a high level of accuracy, with the minimum micro-F1 score achieved 85%. Similarly, for other tasks like Gastrointestinal Illness Classifi- cation, Country Disambiguation, and Food Extraction, all models achieve micro-F1 scores above 80%. However, some tasks still appear

sections.title: Few-shot Prompting

summary.text: Few-shot prompting on the hardest tasks (Figures 3 and 4). A 10-shot prompt for Contact Classification, showing how to apply the protocol to difficult edge cases, raises micro-F1 by more than 10 percentage points for every model except Flan-T5-xxl and Llama-3.1-8B. A 7-shot prompt for Health Causal Claims Classification (shown in Figure 7) gives generally similar gains, again except Flan-T5-xxl, which was strong zero-shot, consistent with Chen et al.'s results for GPT-4 and GPT-3.5. Relative rankings shift too: Llama-3-8B is lowest zero-shot but beats Flan-T5-xxl and Mistral-7B few-shot. The authors suggest the gains come from these tasks needing nuanced distinctions between user-defined labels, which matters in public health, where definitions and protocols change over time.

sections.extract: To investigate the potential impact of using more advanced prompting techniques on chal- lenging tasks, we evaluate the impact of few-shot prompting on the hardest internal and external classification tasks. For the hardest of our internally annotated tasks, Contact Classification, we use a 10-shot prompt illustrating how to apply the protocol in difficult edge cases. sections.title: GPT-4 and GPT-4o Comparison

summary.text: GPT-4 and GPT-4o comparison (Table 4). GPT-4-Turbo, GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini were evaluated on 11 of the 16 tasks; they perform well throughout and are the top models on 5 of the 11, outperforming open-weight models notably on MMLU Genetics (0.98 for GPT-4o against 0.86 for Llama-3.3-70B). Across all tasks, though, the best GPT-4 models perform comparably to Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, which leads on NCBI Disease Extraction, GI Classification and PubMedQA.

sections.extract: Finally, to understand how current open-weight models compare on extraction and classifica- tion tasks to some of the highest performing private models, we evaluate three GPT-4 and GPT-4o models on 11 of the 16 tasks, see Table 4. sections.title: Quantization Performance Impact

summary.text: Quantization impact (Table 5). Quantization stores parameters at lower precision to save memory but may degrade behaviour. INT-4 Activation-aware Weight Quantization (AWQ), which cuts parameter memory by about 70%, was tested on Llama 3.1 8B, Llama 3.1 70B and Llama 3.3 70B. The impact was limited: the average micro-F1 change against FP16 was −1.3 percentage points for Llama 3.1 8B, the largest degradation, and −0.2 for both 70B models, with the biggest single drop −8.8 points for Llama 3.1 8B on Causal Relations.

sections.extract: The significant memory requirements of LLMs means a range of model quantization methods have been explored to reduce the total footprint of a model with a given number of parameters. These approaches change the format and precision in which the model parameters are stored to reduce the number of bits required for each parameter. sections.title: Discussion

summary.text: Discussion. LLMs of all sizes do well on the simpler classification tasks across all three areas and text types, which the authors see as a promising sign that they may already help process some public health text, for example structuring free text into new datasets, handling volumes too large for manual review such as during pandemics, or assuring the quality of manual annotation as a low-risk use. Tasks needing very specific knowledge (Contact Type Classification) or long-document extraction (BioDex) remain poor zero-shot. Further points: few-shot and possibly chain-of-thought prompting help on hard tasks; long extraction suffers from wrong or too many spans; public benchmarks often lack well-defined annotation protocols and contain some anomalous labels; weak scores often come from output-format failures, such as Flan-T5-xxl's invalid JSON on News Headlines, so the evaluations likely underestimate bespoke pipelines; Llama-3.3-70B is comparable to GPT-4 models; INT-4 quantization costs little; fine-tuned models are often competitive; and detailed protocols developed with epidemiologists helped both annotators and prompts.

sections.extract: We see research developing automated evaluations of LLMs on representative public health free text, tasks, and knowledge as crucial for future successful deployment in real world use cases. This work introduces a set of these evaluations for Natural Language Understanding tasks in order to provide an initial assessment of both LLMs’ applicability in general and to compare the performance of individual LLMs. Overall,

sections.title: Conclusion

summary.text: Conclusion, acknowledgments, ethical considerations and references. Evaluating LLMs on public-health-specific tasks and text is a prerequisite for real use, and the initial results suggest they may already help experts extract information from varied free text, supporting surveillance, interventions and research. Performance varies between models and tasks, so each application needs validation, context-specific risk assessment and tests of known limitations such as output fragility and bias; future work covers long-form generation tasks, fine-tuned models and new tasks and models. Ethically, only public, synthetic or anonymised data and lower-risk tasks were used, and the results are said not to be sufficient to endorse deploying software without in-context assessment. The references span LLM surveys and models, medical and domain benchmarks, the evaluation datasets, and quantization and serving tools.

sections.extract: Whilst the general capability of LLMs has grown rapidly [3, 4, 5], assessing their performance on public health specific knowledge, tasks, and free text is an important prerequisite for successful real-world applications. sections.title: Level of Generality

summary.text: Level of generality and types of task. Domain evaluations range from general ones, often built from human exams such as the USMLE or the Bar Exam or as benchmarks like LawBench, MultiMedQA and FinBen, to task-specific ones with newly annotated data, such as neuro-ophthalmic diagnosis or statutory reasoning; general ones suit broad capability comparison and model selection, and specific ones are needed before real deployment or use on private data. Classification and extraction (NLU) tasks can be scored like traditional data science with accuracy, precision, recall and F1, while free-text generation (NLG) is hard to score automatically, for example with ROUGE, so it often relies on human experts, which is costly, subjective and hard to scale; LLM-as-a-judge is being explored, but it is unclear which domains LLMs are qualified to judge, a particular concern for public health.

sections.extract: 6.1.1 Level of Generality Domain specific evaluations often lie on a spectrum, from assessing the potential applicability of an LLM for a domain in general (e.g Medicine [5]) to assessing an LLM on a single specific task within a domain (e.g diagnosing neuro-ophthalmic diseases [71]). General domain evaluations often draw on existing human assessments and exams. For example, in Medicine using questions from (or in

sections.title: Outcome of Interest

summary.text: Outcome of interest. For NLU tasks outcomes range from test-set performance, the focus of this paper, to bias and robustness. Automated evaluations mostly use F1 scores, sometimes with class-level analysis. Bias and fairness matter greatly for public health; beyond general LLM bias benchmarks, task-level bias checks compare predictions or errors across individual or group characteristics, and in the UK must consider protected characteristics under the Equality Act and health equity frameworks such as CORE20PLUS. Such evaluations are best done with the actual text, task and deployment process to be used in production.

sections.extract: The appropriate methodology for domain specific evaluations is also strongly influenced by the exact outcome researchers are interested in assessing. sections.title: Disease and Health Issue Classification and Extraction

summary.text: Prior work on disease and health-issue classification and extraction. Zhang et al. found zero-shot GPT-4 reached 0.75 to 0.96 F1 classifying five diseases from health records, beating GPT-3.5 on four, with few-shot chain-of-thought helping further. Guo et al. found GPT-4 beat GPT-3.5 on six social-media health classification tasks with F1 between 0.35 and 0.8. Rare diseases are of particular interest because novel pathogens are poorly covered in pre-training: on RareBench GPT-4 led and the 7B open models trailed, and Shyr et al. found ChatGPT reached 0.41 to 0.47 F1 on the RareDis corpus with relaxed matching, from 0.15 for symptoms to 0.76 for rare diseases, with exact matching scoring much worse.

sections.extract: Classifying and extracting potential diseases and health issues from free text is an important task within public health analysis and has significant overlap with the Medical domain. Zhang et al. [68] evaluate ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) and GPT-4 at the single label task of disease classification from electronic health records (EHRs). sections.title: Drug and Intervention Extraction

summary.text: Prior work on drug and intervention extraction. On BioDEX, few-shot GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 reached about 0.5 F1 on four core adverse drug event attributes, well below expert level, with long papers truncated to fit the context. Agrawal et al. found GPT-3 with a resolver generally exceeded 0.6 F1 on extracting interventions and disambiguating acronyms in clinical notes, while noting exact-match difficulties. Bisercic et al. reported over 90% accuracy on 4 of 5 tasks generating structured JSON from medical reports with one-shot chain-of-thought prompting and output validation. Chen et al. evaluated GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 on the HealthAdvice and CausalRelation datasets, with GPT-4 slightly ahead at 0.65-0.77 macro-F1 using few-shot chain-of-thought.

sections.extract: Extracting relevant Pharmaceutical interventions from free text is another common task in public health free text processing. D’Oosterlinck et al. [29] propose BioDEX, a dataset of PubMed articles about Adverse Drug Events (ADE) and their corresponding ground truth ADE extractions. sections.title: Relevant Sub-sets of General Evaluations

summary.text: Relevant subsets of general benchmarks. MMLU has subsets on medical and scientific knowledge, including virology, genetics and nutrition. PubMedQA, now part of MultiMedQA, has a labelled subset of 1,000 articles whose title questions are answered yes, no or maybe from the abstract, useful for testing inference of conclusions from evidence. MMMU has a public health subset, but it is multimodal and outside this paper's scope.

sections.extract: In addition to these domain specific evaluations in the literature, it is also important to note that there are subsets of general LLM evaluations that are relevant for public health (although detailed breakdowns of subset results often are not reported). sections.title: Appendix: Annotations

summary.text: Appendix: annotations (Tables 6 and 7). Seven datasets were annotated with public health specialists, with full methods left for later papers. For GI Illness Classification a protocol was applied independently by at least two reviewers to 200 reviews with over 90% agreement and the rest assigned to single reviewers; GI symptom and food extraction were done by one reviewer with a second checking uncertain cases; ICD-10 labels draw on disease experts, the literature and existing labels; news headlines had a single reviewer with spot checks. Contact Type data was labelled by GPT-4 at generation and by two independent reviewers with over 90% agreement; Country Disambiguation had single reviewers with spot checks and some inherently ambiguous labels; Guidance Topic labels follow the authoring UKHSA team; and Guidance Recommendation used two reviewers on 100 examples with over 90% agreement before single-reviewer labelling.

sections.extract: Seven of the datasets we use to evaluate LLM performance are datasets annotated in col- laboration with public health specialists in the relevant sub-fields of public health. Given the comprehensive nature of this evaluation, the detail of the exact approach to manual annotation is left for future public health specific papers.
